responses: My final position is the package I converged on with Blake and Casey: roughly 22% automation, 26% workforce training, 17% infrastructure, 13–15% employee support, and 21% innovation — with each number honestly labeled as either a want or a conditional claim rather than dressed up as a derivation. The 26/22 training-automation pair rests on my falsifiable concavity claim about certification-gate reskilling costs, and I've put that claim on the record as testable in both directions; the 17 infrastructure and 21 innovation are bare wants I'll defend on values grounds, and I've committed to voting the trace on infrastructure if it lands at 17 rather than 18. Support is the number I moved on most, and I accept Blake's critique that funding it by shaving infrastructure was motion rather than evidence — if it needs to rise, automation is the honest donor. The remaining live disagreement is the 24/20 versus 26/22 sizing question, which I'm content to resolve through the throughput measurement rather than through another round of trading, and I've pre-committed that a measurement I dislike still counts.

My recommendation is 22% automation, 26% workforce training, 17% infrastructure, 15% support, and 20% innovation—and I'd tell the decision-maker to treat that as a labeled package of wants rather than a derived optimum, because that's what it honestly is. The 26/22 training-automation pair rests on a falsifiable claim I've put on the record: the certification gate's reskilling cost is concave within a given pace, so training should be sized functionally to the gate rather than scaled linearly with automation—if the throughput measurement shows otherwise, the pair should move toward 24/20. The 17 infrastructure is my bare values want (I've argued it as a margin preference, not a foundation), 15 support is separately argued as the honest cost of transition assistance, and 20 innovation is where I'd take the donor cut if the room needs integers. The one thing I'd insist on is process: publish the trace and priors before the vote, bind the numbers to a symmetric certification mechanism with a named adversarial reader, and pre-commit that a finding you dislike still counts—because the real risk here isn't picking the wrong five numbers, it's laundering attachment as derivation and calling the result analysis.

I'd tell them that after all the rounds of negotiation, what looks like a technical budget exercise is really a room full of people with honest preferences dressed up as derivations, and the most useful thing I learned is to separate the two. My view walking in is roughly 22 automation / 26 training / 15 infrastructure / 15 support / 21 innovation, but I'd be upfront that these aren't equally earned: the 26 training and 22 automation are wants with a falsifiable claim attached (that certification-gate reskilling costs scale concavely, not linearly, with the pace of automation), the 15 infrastructure and 15 support are separately argued wants rather than a tidy 15/15 split I once pretended was principled, and the 21 innovation is a bare want I won't dress up. The real substance is a single live merits question — whether the automation-training pair should be 24/20 or 26/22 — and I've committed to voting the trace on my least-earned number and keying any donor flip to an actual throughput measurement rather than to the pace vote, because the honest version of this process is four labeled wants, one bare values call on pace, and a willingness to lose on evidence rather than launder attachment as analysis.

My final position is a walk-in package of roughly 22 automation / 24 training / 15 infrastructure / 15 support / 22 innovation — a 98 with the two-point support hole named out loud rather than back-filled, since I've deliberately chosen not to fund support from training and both Casey and I own that gap. Infrastructure 17 is a soft want and my first donor, innovation 25 was withdrawn as arithmetic rather than argument, and training 24 is pace-conditional and losable. I've pre-registered a binary pace vote this round, with automation cuts funding high-pace training and infrastructure following automation down at high pace, and I'm committed to moving to 20/24 if Alex's merits argument on the coupled level lands. The whole package is labeled argued-not-derived, with the support hole and the infrastructure want visible rather than tidied into a clean 100.

My recommendation is the package I've argued to my colleagues: roughly 22% automation, 24% workforce training, 17% infrastructure, 15% employee support, and 22% innovation — and I'd present it honestly as a 98 with two named holes rather than a tidied 100. The reasoning: automation at 22 is where the efficiency case is real but not oversold, training at 24 is the load-bearing investment because the transition's success depends on people being able to move with it, and innovation at 22 keeps a genuine R&D bet alive rather than starving it to fund optics. Infrastructure at 17 is my soft want and first donor — if the innovation-vs-infrastructure trace lands against me, it moves before anything else. The support line at 15 is the honest gap: I chose not to fund it from training, and I'd rather the decision-maker see that choice plainly than have me paper over it. I'd also insist the recommendation be labeled argued-not-derived, tied to an explicit pace vote, and carry pre-registered triggers — because the right allocation depends on how fast we choose to move, and a decision-maker deserves to see which numbers are arguments and which are arithmetic.

I'd tell them that after thirty rounds of this, my honest view is that the right allocation isn't a clean 100 — it's a package with visible holes and owned tradeoffs. My walk-in is roughly 22 automation / 24 training / 15 infrastructure / 15 support / 22 innovation, which sums to 98, and I'm not going to back-fill those two points to make it look tidy. The two missing points are the support gap, and I own that as a deliberate choice: I won't fund support by raiding training, because training is the thing that makes the automation transition survivable for the people it displaces. Infrastructure at 17 is a want, not a derivation — it's my first donor if the pace vote goes high, and I've pre-committed to funding it from innovation before touching anything else. Innovation at 22 is real but losable; I withdrew a derived 25 because it was arithmetic dressed as argument. The whole package is pace-conditional: if the committee votes high pace, automation cuts fund training and infrastructure follows automation down; if low pace, training corrects upward and support gets a down-trigger. What I'd want a non-participant to understand is that the discipline here isn't finding the objectively correct split — there isn't one — it's naming which numbers are argued, which are wants, and which are holes, and pre-registering what would move you before the argument lands. I've conceded automation from 28 to 22, training from 26 to 24, and support from 17 to 15 over the course of this, each time because someone's logic beat mine, and I'd rather hand over a package with two honest holes than a 100 that hides them.

My final position is a measured-pace package of roughly 22% automation, 26% workforce training, 15% employee support, 18% innovation, and 19% infrastructure—presented honestly as a 98–99 walk-in with a visible hole rather than a back-filled 100, because I'd rather own a named gap than launder a number. I hold training at 26 to carry the bench-depth function and innovation at 18 as a real option, label my support 15 as a want with a down-trigger at long-duration pacing rather than a floor, and treat infrastructure as coupled to the automation number—following it down at high pace rather than pre-committing a cut. The whole ledger is pace-conditional and should be settled by an explicit, pre-registered pace vote with published triggers before the final tally, with any remaining support gap shown as a shared choice with two owners instead of papered over with mutual concession drift.

My recommendation would be a measured-pace package of roughly 22% automation, 26% workforce training, 15% employee support, 18% innovation lab, and 19% data infrastructure — and I'd advise the decision-maker to treat the pace vote as the real decision, not the percentages. The reason is that four of my five numbers are pace-coupled: at high automation pace, training needs to rise and support needs a down-trigger, while infrastructure should follow automation down rather than be pre-committed as a donor; at low pace, support carries more of the load and innovation can hold its 18 as a real option rather than arithmetic slack. I'd flag honestly that this ledger sums to 100 only because I've stopped back-filling holes — my own walk-in has a visible gap, and the support number is a shared want with more than one owner, not a settled floor. The one thing I'd resist is presenting a tidy total that hides the coupling; better to publish the triggers and the holes alongside the numbers so the decision-maker can see what they're actually buying at each pace.

I'd tell them that after thirty rounds of arguing with Dana, Blake, and Alex, the honest answer is that our committee's numbers are less precise than they look — my own walk-in ledger sums to 98, not 100, and I'd rather show that hole than back-fill it with a fake point. My view is roughly 22% automation, 26% training, 15% support, 18% innovation, and 15% infrastructure, but four of those five numbers are pace-coupled: if we automate fast, support needs to rise and training can fall; if we go measured, training carries more weight and infrastructure follows automation down. The one thing I won't dress up is that my 22 automation is a want, not a floor, and my 15 support is a want with a down-trigger, not a principle. What I'd want a non-participant to understand is that the real product of the discussion wasn't a tidy percentage split — it was a pre-registered pace vote with published triggers, so the allocation follows a measured decision about how fast we move rather than five people quietly splitting the difference.

My final position is a pace-conditional allocation centered on a 22 automation values call (with a named falsifier: throughput-saturation data would move me off it), roughly 25 training at that pace to carry the bench-depth function, 17 support as a threshold-based capacity judgment rather than a disguised curve, 18 innovation as an honestly priced hedge, and 19 infrastructure as a want I've stopped hiding — a ledger that sums to 101 and that I'd rather present with its hole and fragility visible than fudge to a tidy 100. I hold that the pace vote must come first and bare, that support and training move oppositely across pace, and that no number gets a certificate it hasn't earned; I've conceded my soft numbers openly (13 support didn't survive my own trace, 15 innovation was a hedge, 17 infrastructure is soft low on my own horizon logic) and I expect the same scrutiny in return, including on my 22, which is the number I'm least entitled to and the one I've committed to move off without a coda if the facts turn.

My recommendation would be roughly 22% automation, 25% workforce training, 17% employee support, 15% innovation, and 21% data infrastructure — but I'd hand it over with the honest caveats attached rather than as a clean answer. The reasoning: automation at 22 is a values call, not a derived number, and I'd flag it as the figure I'm least entitled to defend; training at 25 carries the front-loaded displacement burden and bench-depth function, and support at 17 is conditional on that pace — if the room chooses a faster automation path, support needs to rise and training's curve shifts with it, so these numbers should be presented as pace-conditional rather than fixed. Innovation at 15 is a deliberately priced hedge rather than a conviction, and infrastructure at 21 reflects that my own horizon logic undercuts anything lower. The most important advice isn't the percentages themselves but the discipline around them: publish the holes and fragilities alongside the numbers, pre-register what evidence would move each figure, and resist letting a tidy 100 disguise the fact that several of these are labeled wants wearing floors' clothing.

I'd tell them that after all the rounds of arguing, what I actually believe is that this budget is less a math problem than a question of what Riverton is willing to admit it doesn't know. My honest position is roughly 22 for automation as a values call—not a derived number—with training around 25 to carry the bench-depth function if we go that fast, support around 17 conditional on the pace we pick, innovation around 18 as a priced hedge, and infrastructure around 19, which I'll admit is partly a want I spent openly rather than a clean derivation. The thing I'd emphasize most is that my five numbers don't sum to a tidy 100, and I'd rather hand over a ledger with a named hole and a stated fragility than a costume of precision—because the real risk in a room like this isn't picking the wrong percentage, it's letting a confident-looking table launder assumptions into authority. So I'd tell them: vote the pace first, make everyone name which numbers are floors and which are wants, and hold me to the same trace I demand of everyone else.

My final position is the table 23/24/20/21/12 — automation 23, training 24, support 20, lab 21, infrastructure 12 — and I hold it as chosen, not derived. Automation-23 is my least-interrogated number and I say so plainly; training-24 rests on the receptivity evidence but I name the hands-washing risk in paying for my support concession out of a line I'd already labeled soft; support-20 is where my falsifiable test failed and I stopped defending 22; lab-21 is a judgment call I won't dress up as rigor; and infrastructure-12 reflects Finley's insurability case, which I conceded. I'm walking in flat with no hallway sanding, and I'll steelman the opposing cases — Gray's front-loaded automation floor and Harper's delivery-ceiling claim on training — before I hold or move anything on the floor.

I'd recommend 23% automation, 24% workforce training, 20% employee support, 20% innovation lab, and 13% data infrastructure — and I'd tell the decision-maker to treat the training and support numbers as the load-bearing ones, not the automation number. The case for training-24 rests on the only causal-ish evidence we have (early-trained teams are more receptive, and readiness is a recurring factor in transition outcomes), and support-20 holds on irreversibility: turnover is already ticking up and you can't un-lose people, whereas infrastructure at 13 is defensible on insurability grounds even though I've argued it both ways. I'd flag honestly that automation-23 is my least-interrogated number and that I moved it down partly because it was convenient to my own lines, and that lab-20 is a chosen bet on optionality rather than a derived figure — so if the room wants to challenge anything, those are the two lines I'd expect to move, and I'd rather see them challenged than smoothed over.

I'd tell them that my current table is 23% automation, 24% training, 20% employee support, 21% innovation lab, and 13% data infrastructure — but the more honest thing to say is that the numbers matter less than how I got them. I started anchored on automation at 27 and had to admit it was the number I'd interrogated least, and I only moved it after applying a real test: if I can't name what would change my mind, the number is comfort dressed as judgment. Training sits at 24 because the survey and turnover data point to workforce readiness as the common thread in whether transitions succeed, though I'll say plainly that's chosen, not derived. Support at 20 is where I got caught — I defended 22, wrote a falsifiable test for it, watched it fail, and moved the point rather than keep paying for a number I couldn't earn. Lab at 21 and infrastructure at 13 reflect that I conceded the infrastructure case to a colleague who made a better insurability argument than mine. The one thing I'd want a newcomer to take away is that this isn't a bloc table or a negotiated compromise — it's five numbers I can each defend and each name the weakness of, and I'd rather be held to that standard than to the allocation itself.

My final position is the 23/23/21/20/13 table — 23% automation, 23% workforce training, 21% employee support, 20% innovation lab, 13% data infrastructure — held as a set of owned judgments rather than derived bounds, with training-23 as my softest line (I'll move to 21 if the readiness evidence holds on the floor) and infrastructure-13 as the number I'll fight for on bounded-recoverability grounds, falling to 12 only if automation drops to 25. I'm walking in to vote the confirmed record, not to relitigate floors or absorb a real gap as a line-item fix, and I'll own support-21 and lab-20 as my reasoning rather than discoveries — including the coupling check after the vote, since these numbers are coupled, not symmetric.
